tests.description: A lone head, tail, grep, or cat of a saved-output path reads the store with no question and writes no copy. A folder from another machine still reads the store by name, and a name not in the store says it is no longer available. Reading a whole saved output back keeps one copy in the store. A chain that also reads a file on disk asks about that file only.

A line that only reads saved output runs in bash with no question, after a copy is written, and prints what the same line prints on a real file with the same text. A copy changed on disk is rewritten from the store before the next line.

awk has no rule, so a read of saved output with it asks std::exec and nothing more, and prints the right lines. A line that only names a saved output still asks a question, std::bash::readonly, because no read of saved output was dropped.

A line safeBash cannot parse gets its copy before bash runs, found by a scan of the text, and a background job gets its copy before it starts. A path inside a longer argument, as in `sh -c 'cat <saved output> | wc -l'`, gets its copy too.
A real program given a saved-output path from another machine's folder fails before any shell starts, with a message that names the path on this machine.

In `touch <file>; cat <saved output>`, the line does more than read, so the cat keeps its std::read question. With std::read rejected the line fails, so an approved write cannot turn into an unasked read.

The shell expands what echo prints, so `echo "$HOME" && wc -l <saved output>` would print what nobody was asked about. A line with any expansion keeps its questions, and with every question rejected it does not run. A variable asks std::env, which is the first question of its line. A glob, a leading `~`, and a glob in a flag's value count as expansions and keep std::read.
With a temp folder whose path has a space, a quoted saved-output path reads with no question. The saved paths come from the parsed words, so no part of the path is taken for a path of its own.
A saved-output folder that other users can use, and a link planted where the folder goes, each fail the line before the shell starts.

A path that continues past a saved-output name is not a saved output: the ordinary rules decide, and a missing file whose folder exists asks std::read for it. A look-alike folder reads the store in process and fails before a real program runs. A redirect into the folder, a delete of a saved output, and a listing of the folder are refused.

The stdlib's read takes a saved-output path as the whole filename, or the folder as dir, with offset and limit, and asks nothing. A folder from another machine reads the store by name. The stdlib's grep searches a saved-output path in the store, and asks nothing. With allowedPaths bound, grep gives the path its ordinary checks and fails, since no copy is on disk.
